title: The Contest Begins: A Staff, a Serpent, and a River of Blood
summary: God tells Moses that he will be like God to Pharaoh, with Aaron as his prophet, and warns that Pharaoh's heart will be hardened. Before Pharaoh, Aaron's staff becomes a serpent; the Egyptian magicians copy the sign, but Aaron's staff swallows theirs. Then, at the bank of the Nile, Aaron strikes the water and it turns to blood, the fish die, and Egypt cannot drink, yet Pharaoh turns away unmoved.
story: The long introduction of chapters 3 to 6 is over, and the confrontation begins. Pharaoh asked in 5:2 who the LORD is; verse 5 gives God's answer in advance: “the Egyptians will know that I am the LORD.” The chapter opens with a preview sign in the throne room and then the first of the plagues, the ten blows that run through chapter 12. The pattern that will repeat is set here: God announces, Moses and Aaron act, Egypt suffers, the magicians respond, and Pharaoh's heart stays hard. Moses, who protested that he could not speak, now stands before the most powerful man in the world with his brother beside him, as God had promised.
historical:
Verse 7 gives Moses' age as eighty and Aaron's as eighty-three, fitting the later picture of Moses' life in three parts, forty years in Egypt, forty in Midian, and forty in the wilderness, ending at 120 (Deuteronomy 34:7). The court scene reflects real Egyptian institutions. The word translated magicians is generally thought to come from an Egyptian title for a lector priest, the learned priest who read the sacred texts in ritual and was credited with knowledge of spells. Such men also interpret Pharaoh's dreams in Joseph's day (Genesis 41:8). Egyptian literature celebrated them. A collection of tales preserved in Papyrus Westcar tells of court magicians who brought a wax crocodile to life and folded back the water of a lake. Much later, Jewish tradition gave names to the magicians who opposed Moses, and Paul uses those names, Jannes and Jambres, in 2 Timothy 3:8.

The Nile was Egypt's life. Nearly all its people lived within a few miles of the river, and its yearly flood, which Egyptians honored as the god Hapi, watered and fertilized the fields. Fish from the river were a staple food. Some readers have linked this plague to an Egyptian text called the Admonitions of Ipuwer, which laments a land in chaos and says that the river is blood. Most Egyptologists, however, date that composition centuries before any proposed date for the exodus and read it as a literary lament over social disorder, not a record of these events.
cultural:
Pharaoh's crown bore the rearing cobra, and Egyptian religion was full of serpent powers, both protective and hostile. The word for serpent in this chapter differs from the one in 4:3. It is the word used for the great sea creatures of Genesis 1:21 and for monsters of the deep, and Ezekiel later calls Pharaoh the “great monster who lies among his rivers” (Ezekiel 29:3). When Aaron's staff swallows the magicians' staffs, the image is of the LORD's power consuming the power Egypt trusted.

Pharaoh going out to the water in the morning (verse 15) may have been for royal inspection of the river or for rites connected with it; the text does not say. What is clear is that the first plague strikes the source of Egypt's life and one of its most honored powers. The river the Egyptians had once used to drown Hebrew babies (1:22) becomes undrinkable. Ezekiel's oracle puts Pharaoh's pride in the words, “The Nile is mine; I made it myself” (Ezekiel 29:3), and this chapter shows whose river it is.
literary: Verses 1 to 7 restate the commission in its final form. Moses will be like God to Pharaoh, and Aaron will be his prophet, which defines a prophet as one who speaks another's words. The plague account that starts here is carefully built. The first nine plagues fall into three groups of three. In each group the first plague is announced to Pharaoh early in the morning, usually at the river (7:15; 8:20; 9:13), the second is announced after Moses goes in to Pharaoh (8:1; 9:1; 10:1), and the third comes without warning (8:16; 9:8; 10:21). The tenth stands apart. Jewish readers noticed the grouping long ago, and the Passover Haggadah, the order of service for the Passover meal, preserves a memory aid attributed to Rabbi Judah that groups the ten as three, three, and four. Within each episode the same elements recur: God's command, the demand to let my people go, the warning, the act, the magicians' response, and the refrain that Pharaoh's heart was hardened and he would not listen, “just as the LORD had said” (verses 13 and 22).

outline.t: Moses like God to Pharaoh, and Aaron his prophet
Aaron's staff swallows the magicians' staffs
The first plague announced at the Nile
The water turns to blood, and Pharaoh turns away

doctrines.note: The plagues are judgments, and the first one falls where Egypt's life and pride were centered. God's judgment in Exodus is measured and announced beforehand, giving warning after warning, and it aims at knowledge: that the Egyptians will know that he is the LORD.

Egypt honored the Nile and its flood as divine gifts and powers. Turning the river to blood shows that it is a creature under the LORD's hand. Idolatry in Scripture is trusting something God made as though it were God, and the plagues take Egypt's trusted powers apart one by one.

God reveals himself in word and deed together. Each plague is announced before it happens, so that the event can be read as the act of the God who spoke. Moses and Aaron are the model of prophetic speech: God's words in a human mouth.

words.note: Tannin, a serpent, and elsewhere a great sea creature or monster. It is a different word from the snake of 4:3, and its range reaches to the creatures of the deep in Genesis 1:21 and to Ezekiel's picture of Pharaoh as a monster in the Nile. When Aaron's staff becomes a tannin and swallows the others, the sign speaks the language of Egyptian power and defeats it.

Chartom, magician. The word is usually traced to an Egyptian title for a lector priest, the learned reader of ritual texts. It appears in the Bible only for the dream interpreters and wonder workers of Egypt and Babylon (Genesis 41; Daniel 1 and 2). These are the most skilled religious experts of the greatest power of the age, and the plague chapters trace their failure.

Kaved, heavy. In verse 14 Pharaoh's heart is heavy, which the BSB renders unyielding. The same root describes God's glory, the weight of his presence, and Exodus plays on the two: Pharaoh's heart grows heavy while God gains glory over him (14:4). Egyptian texts about the judgment of the dead picture the heart weighed on a scale against the feather of truth, and a heavy heart meant condemnation, so the phrase may have carried an extra, ominous sense.

christ: Moses is made “like God to Pharaoh” (verse 1), speaking God's words with God's authority, and Deuteronomy later promises a prophet like him, which Peter applies to Jesus: “You must listen to Him in everything He tells you” (Acts 3:22). Where Moses carries God's word, Jesus is that Word in person. John's Gospel also invites a contrast. The first plague in Egypt turns water into blood and brings death; the first of Jesus' signs, at a wedding in Cana, turns water into wine and brings joy (John 2:1-11). John does not draw the comparison himself, so it should be held as an echo rather than a claim, but it fits the way the New Testament presents Jesus as the one who brings a greater exodus, and not one of judgment on his own people. The plagues also return at the end of the Bible, where Revelation's judgments echo Egypt's: a bowl is poured on the rivers and springs, “and they turned to blood” (Revelation 16:4). The God who judged Pharaoh will judge every power that sets itself against him.

hard.q: How could Pharaoh's magicians copy Moses' signs? Did they have real power?
hard.a:
The text says the magicians did the same things “by their magic arts” (verses 11 and 22), using a Hebrew word that suggests secret or hidden techniques, and it does not explain further. Interpreters have read this in two main ways. Some think of skilled illusion and handling of snakes, arts for which Egyptian practitioners were famous, and of ways to discolor water that was already available (verse 24 notes that water could still be found by digging). Others take the text to mean that the magicians drew on real spiritual power opposed to God, noting that Scripture elsewhere warns of genuine signs used to lead people away from the LORD (Deuteronomy 13:1-3) and of false wonders worked by Satan (2 Thessalonians 2:9).

On either reading the chapter's interest lies elsewhere. The magicians can imitate, but only in ways that make things worse; they can add blood to Egypt, but they cannot turn it back into water. Their serpents are swallowed. By the third plague they fail altogether and confess “This is the finger of God” (8:19), and by the sixth they cannot even stand before Moses (9:11). Whatever their power, it is limited, borrowed, and finally exposed.

questions: The first plague strikes the river Egypt depended on. What are the things our lives depend on so completely that we are tempted to treat them as ultimate?
Pharaoh “did not take any of this to heart” (verse 23). What makes a person able to see clear evidence and still walk away unmoved?
The magicians could imitate God's signs but could not undo the damage. Where have you seen imitations of God's power that promise much and cannot heal?
